source.title_on_document: NarrativeLoom: Enhancing Creative Storytelling through Multi-Persona Collaborative Improvisation

paper_design_summary: Five writers completed formative interviews about AI-supported storytelling (p. 3, Section 3.1). In the main study, 50 analyzed Prolific participants each developed stories from the same initial idea with NarrativeLoom and a single-persona chatbot, both using GPT-4o; presentation was counterbalanced, but random allocation to condition order is not stated (p. 9, Sections 5.1–5.2). Outcomes included computational story features and expert TTCW creativity ratings on a sampled subset reported as 20 story pairs, comprising 40 stories (pp. 10 and 13, Sections 5.3.2, 5.4 and 6.5).

assignment.what_was_assigned: No AI-assistance condition comparison is described; this was a qualitative interview cohort recruited through professional networks.
assignment.quote: We recruited five participants through professional networks to ensure a range of expertise, from emerging writers (2 years) to experienced professionals (15+ years; see Tab. 1).

arms.name: Interview cohort
arms.description: Professional-network recruits discussing their prior AI-writing-tool experiences; no study-provided creative-task intervention (p. 3, Section 3.1).

participants.who: Writers with varied professional narrative-writing backgrounds, all with previous AI-writing-tool use; the qualitative formative sample is separate from the main user study.
participants.quote: We recruited five participants through professional networks to ensure a range of expertise, from emerging writers (2 years) to experienced professionals (15+ years; see Tab. 1).

ai_tool.name_model: Prior AI writing tools; model names not stated for the interview cohort
ai_tool.how_used: Interviewees discussed previous use for brainstorming, research and story development; no AI tool was assigned as a study intervention (p. 3, Sections 3.1.1–3.1.2).

task.description: Semi-structured remote interviews about story-development phases, current AI-tool use, challenges and creative agency; no creative outputs were scored (p. 3, Section 3.1.2).
task.duration: Approximately one hour per interview (p. 3, Section 3.1.2).

studies.label: Main within-subjects storytelling study and expert evaluation

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each participant used NarrativeLoom and the baseline chatbot. System presentation order was counterbalanced; the mechanism assigning participants to orders is not stated. Random story sampling and randomized presentation to expert raters concern evaluation, not assignment of AI assistance.
assignment.quote: We employed a within-subjects design in which participants interacted with both the experimental system (NarrativeLoom) and a baseline system. To mitigate order effects, system presentation was counterbalanced across participants [49].
assignment.locator: p. 9, Section 5.2; p. 10, Section 5.4 (randomization of evaluation material only)

arms.name: NarrativeLoom
arms.description: Multi-persona GPT-4o system: users selected, edited or built on anonymized persona-generated continuations and completed at least two story beats; the same analyzed participants also used the chatbot (p. 9, Sections 5.1–5.2).

arms.name: Chatbot
arms.description: Custom single-persona chatbot using the same model and initial story idea, with direct conversational prompting; these are the same analyzed participants as in NarrativeLoom (p. 9, Sections 5.1–5.2).

participants.exclusions: Of 109 initial recruits, 94 passed the mandatory familiarization test. Participants were excluded if they spent less than 20 minutes interacting with the systems or completed fewer than two story beats in the NarrativeLoom condition, leaving 50 participants for analysis. Counts excluded separately for each reason are not reported. Neither recruitment count is identified as a randomized count; n_randomized remains null (p. 9, Section 5.1).
participants.who: Prolific recruits: native English speakers over 18 years old with at least an undergraduate degree. The final analysis sample followed familiarization and system-use filters. Participants used both systems, so condition counts overlap. Expert evaluation used a sampled subset of their stories, reported as 20 pairs / 40 stories; the number of distinct writers in that subset is not explicitly stated (p. 13, Section 6.5).
participants.quote: This filtering process resulted in a final sample of 50 participants for analysis.
participants.locator: p. 9, Sections 5.1–5.2; pp. 10 and 13, Sections 5.4 and 6.5 (expert-rated subset)

ai_tool.name_model: NarrativeLoom (GPT-4o API) and a custom single-persona chatbot powered by the same model
ai_tool.how_used: NarrativeLoom offers alternative story beats from specialized personas, user selection and editing, and expansion into narrative text; the comparator uses direct conversational prompting with one AI agent (p. 1, Figure 1; p. 9, Section 5.2).

task.description: Develop stories from a participant-created initial idea (sparkle), using the same sparkle with both systems. NarrativeLoom required at least two story beats; users could select, edit or extend suggested continuations (p. 9, Section 5.2).
task.duration: 20 minutes per system following a 3-minute tutorial per system (p. 9, Section 5.2).

outcomes.name: TTCW overall creativity score (total binary tests passed)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Torrance Test for Creative Writing (TTCW): total binary tests passed, from 0 to 14, across the Fluency, Flexibility, Originality, and Elaboration dimensions. Each expert independently made binary pass/fail judgments on the produced stories (p. 10, Section 5.4 and Table 4). Stories were produced during the AI system-interaction sessions (p. 9, Section 5.2); no delayed writing assessment is reported. The paper does not specify how expert ratings were aggregated for the reported paired tests, so unit and n_units remain null. Figure 10 also plots the same score by writer expertise; subgroup values are not tabulated (p. 15, Figure 10).

contrasts.reported: NarrativeLoom M = 9.72 out of 14, SD = 2.1; chatbot M = 5.00 out of 14, SD = 1.8; paired t(79) = 13.68, p < 0.001. Section 6.5 reports four expert raters and a subset of 20 story pairs (40 stories). Section 5.4 describes each expert pair evaluating the same set of 10 story pairs, then reports 20 pairs and 40 stories across expert pairs, leaving the sampling description ambiguous. Each expert independently scored stories, but the paper does not state how those ratings were aggregated for the reported paired test; its analysis unit is therefore left null and t(79) is retained as printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 14, Section 6.5, Quantitative Preference and Creativity Scores; p. 13, Section 6.5 (subset); p. 10, Section 5.4 and Table 4 (scoring and sampling)

outcomes.question: with_ai

The exact total number of analyzed story outputs is not explicitly stated, so n_units remains null; the study-level analyzed people count is retained separately. This is a property of an individual story, not a comparison across writers.

outcomes.name: Expert forced-choice preference for the superior story
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: After TTCW scoring, experts separately selected the story they judged superior in each comparison (p. 10, Section 5.4). The 40 observations are forced-choice judgments/scenarios, coded as ratings, not writers or distinct story pairs (p. 14, Section 6.5). The story-sampling ambiguity described in S2-O1 remains unresolved. Stories were produced during the AI system-interaction sessions (p. 9, Section 5.2).

eligibility.reason: The main study compares two generative-AI configurations within people, but Section 5.2 says only that presentation was counterbalanced and does not specify random assignment to order (p. 9). Random sampling of stories and randomized presentation to expert raters (p. 10, Section 5.4) do not establish randomized AI-assistance assignment. The main study analyzed 50 people (p. 9, Section 5.1), and creativity was scored on produced stories by experts (p. 10, Section 5.4 and Table 4); computational features were also scored on the stories (p. 10, Section 5.3.2; p. 12, Section 6.3). Expert creativity results cover a subset reported as 20 story pairs / 40 stories (p. 13, Section 6.5); its distinct writer count and the aggregation underlying the reported tests are not explicit. Under the short-screening rule, unclear assignment with at least 50 analyzed people and an output-scored outcome requires core = unclear and referral to the two-screener pipeline. The main design is coded other because neither random nor explicitly non-random allocation is established; no observational context classification is inferred. The formative interview study has five participants and no scored creative output (pp. 3–4, Section 3.1 and Table 1).

one_line_finding: In a counterbalanced within-person study with 50 analyzed participants (p. 9, Sections 5.1–5.2), the expert-rated story subset favored NarrativeLoom over the chatbot on overall TTCW creativity (M = 9.72, SD = 2.1 versus M = 5.00, SD = 1.8; t(79) = 13.68, p < 0.001; p. 14, Section 6.5), while random assignment to condition order remains unstated.
